title: Col. Stephen Trigg of Viney Grove
summary: Stephen Trigg settled Trigg’s Station near Harrodsburg, served as Lincoln County’s militia colonel, and was killed at Blue Licks on August 19, 1782.
bodyMarkdown:
Stephen Trigg (c. 1744–1782) was a Virginia frontier official and militia officer who moved to Kentucky during the Revolution. He helped settle land claims, served in early county government, and died leading men at the Battle of Blue Licks in 1782. Trigg County carries his name.

## A Virginia frontier official

An account of [Stephen Trigg](https://grokipedia.com/page/stephen_trigg) describes a man from a prominent family on the Virginia frontier who was reportedly among its wealthiest residents. He served as a justice in Botetourt, Fincastle and Montgomery counties. He was also a member of the Fincastle committee that drafted the Fincastle Resolutions of January 1775, an early statement of colonial resistance.

## The land court

In 1779 Virginia named Trigg one of four judges on a land court sent to sort out Kentucky claims. The court's arrival itself drew new emigration of people seeking titles. In all, the court judged 1,328 claims covering more than a million acres.

After the sessions, Trigg stayed. He set up his home on 1,000 acres at Trigg's Station, about four miles north-west of Harrodsburg. The [Kentucky Historical Society marker for Trigg County](https://history.ky.gov/markers/county-named-1820) says he came to Kentucky in 1779 and settled the station in 1780. The [James Harrod Trust's page on the site](https://www.jamesharrodtrust.org/tours/rural-mercer-driving-tour/stephen-triggs-station/) says it was also known as Haggin's Station, Gordon's Old Station and Viney Grove.

## Lincoln County

When Kentucky County was split in 1780, Trigg became lieutenant colonel of the Lincoln County militia, and in 1781 its colonel. He was one of the first justices of the peace and a trustee for laying out Louisville. In the Virginia House of Delegates he and [John Todd](/stories/col-john-todd-of-lexington/) secured passage of the act creating the town of Louisville.

## Blue Licks

In August 1782 a Shawnee raiding party led by British and Loyalist officers struck [Bryan Station](/stories/bryan-station-siege-august-1782/) and withdrew. Todd and Trigg [rallied](https://grokipedia.com/page/Battle_of_Blue_Licks) about 182 militiamen to pursue them. That account calls Trigg "Lieutenant Colonel" in some passages and "Colonel" in others. Trigg commanded the right wing and Daniel Boone the left.

The militia was routed at the [Battle of Blue Licks](/stories/battle-of-blue-licks/) on August 19, 1782. Trigg was among the dead, and when troops returned his body was found quartered. He was buried in a mass grave near the battlefield, in present Nicholas County.

## Kentucky today

Trigg County was formed in 1820 and named for him, but sources differ on the details. It was taken from Christian and Caldwell counties, according to the Kentucky Historical Society and another account. One account [names Christian and Logan in one place](https://grokipedia.com/page/Trigg_County,_Kentucky) and Christian and Caldwell in another, and gives both January 27 and December 27, 1820 as the formation date. A historical marker stands on the courthouse lawn in Cadiz.
